emails.subject: Mailbox Near Quota – Action Required
emails.body:
Your mailbox is currently at 92% of its storage quota. Please review and clear older messages to ensure continued delivery.

BrambleMail capacity notice for Elena Varma at Docklight Exhibits. The figure in the first line is the current reading: 92 percent of the mailbox quota.

How the reading is taken. The quota job runs each morning and writes the percentage, the mailbox size, and the size of the largest folders. This morning the mailbox was at 92 percent. Inbox is the largest folder. Sent and trash are small. The job does not delete anything. It only sends this notice when the reading crosses 90 percent.

The last month of readings, from the same job. 18 March, 71 percent. 25 March, 76 percent. 1 April, 81 percent. 8 April, 86 percent. 16 April, 90 percent, which is the notice that asked for a review before the end of that day. 18 April, 91 percent. 20 April, 91 percent, with the warning that a full mailbox can bounce new mail. 21 April, this notice, 92 percent.

On 16 Apr 2026, IT Notifications <it@docklightexhibits.com> wrote:
> Storage is nearly full.
> Clearing non-essential mail will help avoid delivery issues this afternoon.
> The quota job will write again in the morning.

IT has not placed a hold on the account and has not raised a ticket beyond the automatic notice. Delivery is still succeeding. The notice asks Elena to review older messages so that a later, fuller reading does not start bouncing new mail. The helpdesk address on the footer can explain the quota. It does not file mail for her.

-- BrambleMail notifications
Docklight Exhibits IT

Operator detail behind the BrambleMail notice "Mailbox Near Quota – Action Required" sent 2026-04-21 by IT Notifications. The percentage or the warning in the first line is the reading from the quota job that morning. The job measures the mailbox, writes a line, and sends a notice when the reading is over the threshold. It does not move mail.

Each morning's notice is its own message, with its own subject, because the template changes the subject as the reading climbs. Inbox is the folder that accounts for almost all of the used space. Trash is emptied by a nightly job and does not change the percentage. Sent mail is small.

The six-month line, where a notice mentions one, is the template's suggestion, and Docklight keeps exhibitor contracts in the project folders rather than in this mailbox.

Elena's side of it. She was on the road for the two weeks these notices accumulated. They waited in the inbox next to the older show mail, the newsletters, and the delivered-shipment notes. emails.subject: Spring Booth AV Package – 20% Off (Expires Mar 2025)
emails.body:
Book a full AV package for any spring 2025 show and save 20%. Offer expired March 31, 2025.

ProAV Rentals, a spring discount that expired on 31 March 2025.

The offer was 20 percent off a full booth AV package for any spring 2025 show, if booked by that date. The date passed. The discount code does not price. Docklight's AV for the shows that spring was drawn from our own crates, and the delivery notice for those crates is a different message. This one is the rental house's expired promotion. No quote number was issued.

What 'full AV package' meant in their words. A projector, a screen, two speakers, a small mixer, and the cases, delivered to a show dock and collected at strike. The 20 percent applied to that list. After 31 March 2025 the same list is at the ordinary rate, and only if someone asks. Nobody has asked.

On February 2025, ProAV Rentals <promo@proavrentals.com> wrote:
> Spring booth AV, 20 percent off, for shows in spring 2025.
> Book by 31 March 2025.
> After that date the offer is withdrawn.

31 March 2025 passed and the offer was withdrawn.

ProAV Rentals

The long form of the campaign behind "Spring Booth AV Package – 20% Off (Expires Mar 2025)", as ProAV Rentals sent it on 2025-04-06. Marketing mail of this shape is a headline, a price or a date, and a button. The paragraphs above are that offer. The notes below are the terms that were on the landing page the button pointed at.

Terms that were on the page. The price or the seat they name was a campaign price, good for the window printed in the mail, and withdrawn when the window closed. A code in the mail prices only inside that window. Outside it, the page either says the offer has ended or shows the ordinary list price. No account was opened by receiving the mail, and no invoice was raised because nobody completed an order on the page.

Who it was aimed at. The list is people who had once downloaded a checklist, attended a webinar, or sat on a conference announcement list. The greeting uses a first name when they have one and a generic hello otherwise. ProAV Rentals is the sender on the campaign, and the footer is how they tell a reader the message is promotional. The preference link changes this list only.

What a reply would have done, at the time. A reply to the campaign address reached a mailbox that collects bounces and the occasional human question about the offer. It did not reach a salesperson with our file open, because there was no file. The campaign report for this send shows delivery to the address and no click that turned into a booking.

Record line their tool stored with the send. Date 2025-04-06. Subject "Spring Booth AV Package – 20% Off (Expires Mar 2025)". Result: delivered. Subsequent state: the window named in the copy has passed, and the same tool is not retrying the offer. The message stayed in the inbox because nobody moved it.

Top stories from September 2025: booth design trends, labor shortages, and venue updates across North America.

Expo Weekly, the September 2025 roundup. A newsletter. The three items in the first line are the stories, and the blurbs are below.

Booth design trends. A survey of island booths from that season's shows, with notes on lower walls and open corners. The photos are from public show floors. Docklight is not named.

Labor shortages. A report on rigging and electrical labor in three cities that autumn, with the rates the venues were quoting then. Those rates were for that season's calls. The piece does not ask for a booking.

Venue updates across North America. Renovations announced by four halls, with reopen dates that have since passed or been published on the halls' own sites. The roundup is a digest of those announcements.

Expo Weekly sends this monthly. Unsubscribe is on the footer. Nothing in the September issue is an invoice or a hold on a booth.
